a-call-to-action.title: Agile Practice Guide call to action
a-call-to-action.notes: Agile adoption has grown sharply since the 2001 Manifesto and is no longer limited to IT or particular organisation sizes; inspection, adaptation and transparency remain constant truths; readers are invited to experiment, give feedback and engage with PMI and Agile Alliance communities ('inspection without adaptation is wasted effort'). Short orientation only - no examinable detail beyond reinforcing inspect-adapt-transparency.

a-pmbok-ka-mapping.title: Applying agile across the PMBOK Guide Knowledge Areas (Annex A1)
a-pmbok-ka-mapping.notes: Table A1-1 repeats the 49-process Process Group/Knowledge Area mapping (consistent with PMBOK Table 1-4, already verified). Table A1-2, per Knowledge Area: Integration - team members act as local domain experts deciding how plans and components integrate; the PM's expectations do not change, but detailed product planning and delivery are delegated to the team; PM builds a collaborative decision-making environment; broad skill bases help. Scope - less time defining scope up front, more on establishing a process for ongoing discovery and refinement; prototypes and releases refine requirements; scope is defined and redefined throughout; the requirements constitute the backlog. Schedule - short cycles with review and adaptation; iterative and on-demand pull-based scheduling; large organisations may need roadmaps and scaling factors (team size, geography, regulatory, organisational and technical complexity) and hybrid techniques; the PM's role does not change but they must know adaptive tools. Cost - lightweight high-level estimation of labour costs, detailed estimates just in time for short horizons; with strict budgets, scope and schedule are adjusted to stay within cost. Quality - frequent quality and review steps throughout rather than at the end; retrospectives check quality process effectiveness, find root causes and trial improvements; small batches uncover inconsistencies early when change is cheaper. Resources - self-organising teams of generalising specialists; collaboration critical with high variability; physical and human resource planning less predictable, so fast-supply agreements and lean methods matter. Communications - more frequent, faster communication; streamlined access to information, frequent checkpoints, colocation, transparent artefacts and regular stakeholder reviews. Risk - frequent reviews of incremental work and cross-functional teams; risk considered when selecting iteration content and managed each iteration; requirements are a living document reprioritised by risk exposure. Procurement - sellers may extend the team; shared risk-reward models; a master services agreement for the overall engagement with adaptive work in an appendix or supplement so it can change without affecting the overall contract. Stakeholders - direct engagement rather than through management layers; co-creative exchange among client, user and developer; regular interaction mitigates risk and builds trust; 'aggressive transparency' (open meetings, public artefacts) surfaces misalignment and dependencies early.

a-manifesto-mapping.title: Agile Manifesto values and principles mapped to the Agile Practice Guide (Annex A2)
a-manifesto-mapping.notes: Table A2-1 (rendered): individuals and interactions over processes and tools -> 4.2 servant leadership, 4.3 team composition, 5.1 chartering, 5.2.4 daily standups, 6.2 culture; working software over comprehensive documentation -> 5.2.2 backlog preparation, 5.2.3 refinement, 5.2.5 demonstrations/reviews, 5.2.7 execution practices; customer collaboration over contract negotiation -> 4.3, 5.4 measurements, 6.2, 6.3 procurement and contracts, 6.7 structure; responding to change over following a plan -> 5.2.1 retrospectives, 5.2.3, 5.2.5. Table A2-2 lists the twelve principles (customer satisfaction through early, continuous delivery; welcome changing requirements; deliver frequently, preferring shorter timescales; business and developers work together daily; build around motivated individuals and trust them; face-to-face conversation is most efficient; working software is the primary measure of progress; sustainable pace; technical excellence and good design; simplicity - maximising work not done; self-organising teams produce the best architectures, requirements and designs; regular reflection and adjustment) with section cross-references. The principle-to-section column alignment in the extracted text is not reliable; lessons use the principles themselves (already covered in APG 2.2) and cite Annex A2 generally rather than individual row mappings.

a-frameworks-team.title: Agile and lean frameworks: selection criteria, Scrum, XP, Kanban Method, Crystal, Scrumban, FDD, DSDM, Agile UP
a-frameworks-team.section: APG Annex A3.1-A3.9 (Figures A3-1 to A3-5, Tables A3-1 to A3-5)
a-frameworks-team.notes: No framework is mandatory; an approach built from scratch is fine if it follows the Manifesto's values and principles. Frameworks included are holistic, formalised for common use and popular (industry surveys). Fig A3-1 plots approaches by breadth of life cycle coverage and depth of guidance (team methods vs scaled approaches). Scrum: single-team framework of roles, events, artefacts and rules; sprints are consistent timeboxes of 1 month or less producing a potentially releasable increment; events: sprint, sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, sprint retrospective; artefacts: product backlog, sprint backlog, increments; roles: product owner (maximises product value), development team (cross-functional, self-organising, has everything needed), scrum master (upholds the process, coaches, removes impediments). XP (Table A3-2, rendered): practices grouped by area - organisational (primary: sit together, whole team, informative workspace; secondary: real customer involvement, team continuity, sustainable pace), technical (pair programming, test-first programming, incremental design; secondary: shared code/collective ownership, documentation from code and tests, refactoring), planning (user stories, weekly cycle, quarterly cycle, slack; secondary: root cause analysis, shrinking teams, pay per use, negotiated scope contract, daily standups), integration (10-minute build, continuous integration, test-first; secondary: single code base, incremental deployment, daily deployment); core values communication, simplicity, feedback, courage, respect. Kanban Method: from lean manufacturing (Taiichi Ohno, Toyota, 1953); 'kanban' means visual sign or card; board as information radiator with columns for work states (simplest: to do, doing, done); 'start where you are', less prescriptive, no prescribed timeboxes; pull single items and limit WIP; suited to flexibility needs, continuous delivery, productivity and quality via WIP limits, efficiency, focus, variable workload and waste reduction; defining principles - start with current state, agree to pursue incremental evolutionary change, respect current process, roles and titles, encourage leadership at all levels; core properties - visualise workflow, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, improve collaboratively; completing work matters more than starting new work (Fig A3-2 board with doing/done sub-columns and WIP limits). Crystal (Fig A3-3, rendered): family scaled by number of people and criticality (defects cause loss of comfort, discretionary money, essential money or life); Crystal Clear (1-4 people), Yellow (6-20), Orange (20-40), Red (the next band, printed '5-100' on the axis - likely 50-100; lessons avoid quoting that figure); core values people and interaction, community, skills, talents, communications; common properties frequent delivery, reflective improvement, close/osmotic communication, personal safety, focus, easy access to expert users, technical environment with automated tests, configuration management and frequent integration. Scrumban: started as a transition from Scrum to Kanban, now a hybrid - Scrum framework plus kanban boards and WIP limits for improvement; daily meetings; a planning trigger when WIP falls below a limit; no predefined roles. FDD: built for a large software project; features are small business-valued capabilities; six roles (project manager, chief architect, development manager, chief programmer, class owner, domain expert); five iterative activities (develop overall model, build features list, plan by feature, design by feature, build by feature); supporting practices include domain object modelling, individual class ownership, feature teams, inspections, configuration management, regular builds, visibility of progress. DSDM (Fig A3-5, rendered): constraint-driven delivery - traditional approach fixes features and varies time and cost; DSDM fixes cost, time and quality and varies functionality through formal prioritisation; eight principles - focus on the business need, deliver on time, collaborate, never compromise quality, build incrementally from firm foundations, develop iteratively, communicate continuously and clearly, demonstrate control. Agile UP: lighter, faster offshoot of the Unified Process; disciplines model, implementation, test, deployment, configuration management, project management, environment; principles - the team knows what it's doing, simplicity, agility, focus on high-value activities, tool independence, tailoring to fit, situationally specific.

a-frameworks-scaled.title: Scaling frameworks: Scrum of Scrums, SAFe, LeSS, Enterprise Scrum, Disciplined Agile
a-frameworks-scaled.notes: Scrum of Scrums ('meta Scrum'): two or more Scrum teams of three to nine members coordinate; a representative from each meets, typically two to three times a week (potentially daily), reporting completed work, next work, current impediments and upcoming impediments that might block other teams; large programmes can add a Scrum of Scrum of Scrums (Fig A3-6). SAFe: a knowledge base of patterns for scaling across all levels of the enterprise; principles begin with take an economic view, apply systems thinking, assume variability and preserve options, build incrementally with fast integrated learning cycles, base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems (continues on PDF 921).
